transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-30
Time: 16:00 UTC (52 minutes)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (CTO - Hemisphere Tech), Emily Zhang (ML Eng), Jared Brooks (Platform), Sara Klein (Security)

Summary: quick preview of Redwood API parity options for swapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together, focus on cost parity, streaming/embeddings differences, console demo of routing and optimize suggestions, and next steps for a pilot.

Topics: parity mapping, tokenization diffs, embeddings compatibility, KV cache/continuation, VPC/private deployment options, security (SOC2/KMS/SAML), cost forecasts and reserved capacity, pilot scope.

[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing this in. quick intros then we’ll jump into a short live demo.
[00:18] Noah Patel (CTO): yep thanks, we have like 50 mins ish. curious mostly about cost parity and how much we need to change our endpoints.
[00:27] Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE): awesome. I’ll focus on parity mapping, API differences, and a quick Console tour of the Optimize suggestions; Priya will show the pilot template.
[00:35] Emily Zhang (ML Eng): hi all, emily here — we run two main endpoints: chat completions (OpenAI style) about 1.2M tokens/day and embeddings for search ~120k req/month.
[00:48] Jared Brooks (Platform): also interested in VPC/on-prem options — some regulated customers demand private networking.
[00:54] Sara Klein (Security): and SOC2, SSO, KMS questions — we’ll want to see the docs.

[02:00] Diego: quick agenda — 1) parity mapping for chat + embeddings, 2) Console/Optimize cost sim, 3) routing/fallback and dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, 4) pilot ask. sound good?
[02:15] Noah: yep go for it.

[04:05] Diego: ok starting with chat parity — typical differences we see: streaming tokenization chunking, stop sequences, function calling semantics vary across vendors. On Redwood API we provide a thin adapter so your existing client can call with minimal change — simple mapping for model names and a small shim for streaming deltas. For Anthropic/Together there are some shape differences; we map those in the parity spreadsheet I’ll share.
[04:50] Emily: when you say shim, do we need to re-tokenize? Our embedding pipeline relies on exact token ids for caching.
[05:03] Diego: good question. in most cases tokenization is deterministic across open-source tokenizers but there are edge cases; we’ll run your token logs and produce a tokenization diff report. for KV cache preservation you can either use our prefix-KV compatibility layer or rehydrate cache keys via a simple adapter — both are in the migration checklist.

[07:22] Maya: quick demo time — Priya, can you share your screen and open the Console?
[07:30] Priya Nair (Redwood SE): sharing now — tell me if anything is fuzzy, my wifi is meh today.
[07:42] [screen share starts]
[07:45] Priya: here’s the Console project — we’ve preloaded an example parity mapping for OpenAI-chat -> redwood/gpt-8-mini (note: names are illustrative). On the right you can see Optimize suggestions: batching window suggestions, quantization profiles, and prefix caching settings.
[08:10] Emily: how are the cost savings estimated? is that token-level or per-host?
[08:20] Priya: token-level model cost plus amortized infra — the estimator uses your token distribution or a default traffic profile. there’s a toggle to simulate reserved capacity discounts and burst pricing. you can upload a csv of your traffic shape and it will recompute.

[10:12] Diego: highlighting routing — you can set a policy to prefer hosted low-latency model for interactive routes and fall back to cheaper quantized model for batch edges; that’s a common pattern to hit cost parity. So you essentially keep the same API surface but change model variants behind the scenes.
[10:40] Jared: for embeddings — any vector dimension mismatches we need to worry about? we use 1536 dims today.
[10:50] Diego: our embeddings mapping supports multiple dims; if you need exact numeric parity we recommend running a small equivalence test — the embedding similarity delta report in the parity bundle. we also provide an embedding post-processor to normalize cosine scaling.

[13:05] Noah: what about latency — our SLAs are 200ms p95 for chat in prod. compare hosted vs dedicated?
[13:15] Maya: hosted can hit 200ms for smaller models in low contention; dedicated gives you predictable throughput with GPU pools. the Console shows p95 estimates based on your sequence length distribution. for strict SLOs customers often reserve capacity + burst to guarantee 200ms.

[15:00] Diego: small aside — some transcription funny bits, we often see customers say KV "cash" — it’s KV cache.., just to be clear.
[15:08] Emily: (laughs) yeah we say cash too in Slack.

[16:20] Priya: walking through an example parity mapping file — sample lines: source_model: "gpt-4o" -> redwood_model: "rwd-gpt4o-compat"; streaming shim: "delta_to_event"; stop sequence mapping: remove or reapply depending. you can override per route.
[17:02] Diego: and for function calling — we have a fallback translator for different function call payload shapes, but we recommend normalizing on your side for complex schemas. the translator is good for quick onramp.

[19:30] Noah: ok the thing that will make our execs nervous is cost. can you walk through a quick example with our numbers?
[19:40] Priya: sure — using Emily’s numbers — chat 1.2M tokens/day, embeddings 120k req/month. toggling the reserved capacity slider to a 3-month commit cuts per-token model cost by about 28% in this sim; using quantized variants for batch jobs trims infra by another 15-20%. combined we can show a projected cost parity or modest savings vs your current spend depending on commit level.
[20:15] Emily: is quality impacted much with quantized variants for chat? we have a few sensitive flows.
[20:25] Diego: for high-sensitivity flows we recommend keeping the top-tier float model and using quantized smaller models for non-critical or batch. we also support A/B rollouts and automatic quality regressions tied to your eval sets — Console will alert if embedding similarity or answer quality drops beyond a threshold.

[22:05] Sara (Security): about private deployment — is the control plane still hosted? how do audit logs flow to our SIEM?
[22:18] Maya: for Redwood Private we ship a control plane that can be customer-managed in your VPC; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via secure delivery. we also support customer KMS/HSM for key material. we’ll attach SOC2/ISO artifacts and an architecture diagram.
[22:35] Sara: we’ll need SAML SSO and RBAC integration as well, and a data retention policy that we can set per project.
[22:43] Diego: yep, those are standard. we also keep per-token tracing hooks if you opt in for debugging — you can redact at token-level for PII.

[24:00] [30s overlap, mild crosstalk]
[24:20] Emily: about the tokenization diff — how do we get that produced? what logs do you need?
[24:32] Diego: a sample of request payloads and the tokenizer outputs ideally. if you can drop a few thousand example requests or our script can sample from your endpoint. we’ll run an automated diff and produce a report showing mismatched token boundaries and a suggested adapter.

[26:02] Maya: sharing the migration checklist — high level steps: 1) run tokenization diff, 2) map endpoints and function call shapes, 3) pilot on dedicated vs hosted to gather p95/throughput, 4) iterate model variants for cost/perf, 5) rollout with canary and fallback.
[26:40] Noah: timeline wise, if we started the pilot in mid-June how long to full lift? we have a Q3 product release so need migration done before early Sept.
[26:52] Diego: typical pilot runs 2-4 weeks for baseline + 2-6 weeks for parity fixes; end-to-end could be 6-10 weeks depending on complexity. mid-June pilot + July fixes + August staged rollout would be feasible.

[29:00] Priya: demoing the Optimize feature — you can upload token distribution csv and we’ll auto-suggest batching window (ms), prefix cache policy, and quantization profile. clicking "simulate" gives you estimated cost delta and p95 changes.
[29:38] Emily: can we tie optimize suggestions to CI so that every model change recommends updated settings?
[29:48] Priya: yes, there’s a suggestions API and a webhook you can use in your CI to gather and apply suggested configs.

[31:55] Diego: question from our side — what are your success metrics for this migration? is cost-only, or quality+latency too?
[32:08] Noah: cost is primary but quality must be within 2-3% on our eval sets and latency p95 must be below 250ms.
[32:15] Emily: and embedding similarity for search should be >0.98 of baseline on our holdout.

[33:40] Diego: noted — those are measurable and we can attach regression alerts. Console will run evals against your prompt set.

[35:00] Maya: ok some common objections — vendor lock, model drift, and compliance. our recommendation: keep model-agnostic adapter layer, short canaries, and guard rails; we provide both hosted and private so you can choose posture.
[35:22] Noah: vendor lock is real — can you migrate back if needed?
[35:28] Diego: yes, because we don't require proprietary model changes on your client; adapters live in your infra (or ours) and are reversible. plus we can export a mapping pack for roll-back.

[37:10] Emily: gotcha — small nit: Together’s sampling seeds are different; any gotchas with determinism for tests?
[37:22] Diego: seeding can differ across runtimes; we recommend sampling-based parity tests rather than exact token match for nondeterministic outputs. where determinism is needed, run tests with fixed seeds and a specific model variant that supports deterministic decode.

[39:00] Maya: wrapping up the demo — I’ll drop the parity mapping spreadsheet, pilot template, and pricing deck after this call.
[39:12] Noah: appreciated. one last thing — support SLAs and on-call for incidents during pilot?
[39:20] Maya: included for Dedicated and higher tiers, and we can do a short-term support add-on for the pilot.

[41:05] Priya: demo end — quick note: we’ve linked a sample adapter repo in the Console "resources" panel (note: it’s a short repo link, not full code here).

[42:00] Sara: about security docs — please send the SOC2 report and our team will run a gap analysis.
[42:10] Maya: will do — I’ll add that to action items.

[44:30] Noah: ok next steps recap?
[44:38] Maya: sure — 1) we’ll send pricing and reserved options, 2) Diego sends parity spreadsheet + sample adapter, 3) Hemispher team shares two endpoints and token logs, 4) Priya sets up pilot in Console and invites you, 5) Sara will review security docs.
[45:05] Emily: thanks.

[46:20] [brief silence, loose chat] Jared: also curious about cost of per-request tracing vs token-only logging — how much overhead?
[46:35] Diego: tracing adds small overhead to storage and a tiny latency bump if you opt-in, but you can sample traces to keep costs minimal. Console will show estimated overhead.

[48:00] Maya: anything else?
[48:06] Emily: nope all good.

[49:30] Noah: we’ll review the materials and aim to get you the endpoints by next Friday.
[49:40] Maya: perfect, thanks everyone. we’ll follow up in email with dates for pilot kick-off.

[51:10] Diego: quick FYI — I’ll include a note about the tokenizer script and an example command to produce token logs.
[51:30] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.

Meeting end.
